plan.title: The Toll Booth on Verrin Point Bridge Never Closes
plan.characters: Nell Harlan (narrator, 24): broke, desperate for work, practical, takes the night job on a dare from her rent. Walter Pruitt (60s): soft-spoken day manager who hires her, always calm, always carrying a thermos. Teddy Marsh (30s): the previous night attendant, supposedly 'quit' 19 days ago. His jacket still hangs in the booth, and his handwriting fills the ledger.
plan.setting: The toll booth at the east end of Verrin Point Bridge, a two-lane bridge over a wide, fogbound river in the fictional town of Ashgrove. The bridge is 'open for maintenance traffic' from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Almost no one lives nearby. The far end of the bridge disappears into fog. The booth holds a brass coin drawer, a landline phone, a heavy ledger, a laminated rules card and a bell on a pole that rings at 6 a.m. The toll is $1.50, coins only.

parts.events: Nell starts her first night. Pruitt gives her a laminated card of rules: 1) Every car pays, coins only, no change. 2) Log time, plate and passengers in the ledger before lifting the gate. 3) Never look in the back seat. The driver holds up fingers for the passenger count. 4) At 3:10 the gate arm lowers itself. Leave it. 5) Drivers never get out. If someone knocks on the glass, it isn't a driver. 6) Don't leave the booth until the 6 a.m. bell. Before he goes, Pruitt has her 'sign in' on the first line of a fresh ledger page. The printed columns read Name and Passengers, and she writes 'N. Harlan, 1' without thinking. Teddy Marsh's jacket still hangs on the hook. Cars start arriving with no engine sound, each with a driver silently holding up fingers. Their coins are ice cold and dripping river water, and some are dated before 1960. At 3:10 the gate arm lowers by itself, and a knock sounds on the booth glass.
parts.cliffhanger: The knocking stops. A wet, shaky voice comes through the glass: 'Nell? It's Teddy. Please, it's freezing. Let me in.' Pruitt told her Teddy quit three weeks ago, and she has never told anyone her name tonight.

parts.events: Nell doesn't answer. Wet handprints appear on the outside of the glass, circling the booth. When she stays silent, Teddy writes in the fog on the window, backwards so she can read it: 'THE BOOK. FIRST LINE.' She finds Teddy's old notes taped under the coin tray: 'The count must balance. Mine didn't.' A car arrives at 3:40 with its rear windows fogged from inside by dozens of small handprints. The driver holds up zero fingers, but the drawer fills with seven coins. She flips back through the ledger and sees that every keeper's first line reads the same as hers: 'Passengers: 1'. The ink on Teddy's first line has a thin line struck through it. Hers hasn't been struck.
parts.cliffhanger: At 4:12 headlights roll up to the gate. It is Nell's own green hatchback, which she left in the employee lot. The driver wears her coat, and her face is a pale smear. She holds up one finger.

parts.events: The gate arm stays down, and the car idles with no engine sound. The driver mouths 'lift it'. A hand reaches out the window holding Nell's lucky 1998 quarter, which she had in her pocket. Her pocket is empty. Nell grabs the booth landline and calls Pruitt at 4:20 a.m.; he answers on the first ring, wide awake. She tells him everything, and he asks only one question: 'Did you sign the first line?' Silence. Then he says quietly, 'I'm sorry, I thought you'd ask more questions before you signed. I didn't. Neither did I.' Outside, headlights appear behind her car, a line of old cars stretching back across the bridge, every driver holding up a finger toward her booth. The fog at the far end thickens and slides closer.
parts.cliffhanger: Pruitt says, 'Don't lift that gate for your own car, whatever you do, and don't let the bell find you in it,' then the line goes dead. A single chime of the bell rings out over the bridge, an hour and a half early.

parts.events: Nell breaks rule five on purpose and opens the booth door. Teddy stands there soaked and gray, not threatening, just exhausted. He explains what he knows: the bridge is a crossing for the dead, who drive in their last cars to a far shore that has no road. The keeper counts them through so the ledger balances. The sign-in line is a ticket: whoever is on the first line goes across at the bell, in their own car, unless the line is cancelled. Pruitt got out by getting Teddy to sign. Teddy tried to walk off at 5:59 without a replacement, and the bridge voided him, leaving him uncounted, unable to cross or to leave, walking the bridge every night for 19 days. He can't cross because he has no coin; he lost it in the river. Nell's quarter, the one her double offered, is now in the drawer. Teddy says there is one way to cancel her ticket: she has to write his name in the passenger line, in ink, and say the count out loud, so he rides in her car instead of her. The bridge will take whoever fills the seat. The catch is that the signature still binds her as keeper.
parts.cliffhanger: Before Nell can answer, the booth floor starts shaking, and every handprint on the glass lights up pale in the headlights. The bell rings a second time, and her car's passenger door swings open by itself.

parts.events: Nell weighs her options for a few seconds and decides. She picks up the pen, writes 'Teddy Marsh' on the passenger line, and says 'one' out loud. She hands Teddy her lucky quarter as his toll. He thanks her, steps out of the booth, and climbs into the passenger seat of her car. The gate arm lifts on its own. The hatchback rolls forward into the fog with Teddy inside and the driver gone, and the ledger line closes itself with a dry pop of ink. The long line of old cars moves again and all of them cross, every driver holding up the right number of fingers now. At 6:00 the bell rings once, and her ticket is clear. Pruitt arrives with his thermos and reads the ledger. He tells her she balanced it on her first night and that Teddy took two years to learn. She says she's quitting. He just looks at her hands. When she drives away she makes it to town, and by dusk she finds herself back in the booth with the card in her hand and no memory of the walk.
parts.cliffhanger: A month later, a kid named Eli Brandt turns up for the night shift, desperate for work like she was. Nell hands him the laminated card and the open ledger, smiles the way Pruitt did, and says, 'Just print your name on the first line, Eli, and leave passengers as one.'

plan.reveal: Verrin Point Bridge is a crossing for the dead, and it needs a living keeper to count them over. The keeper's sign-in line is secretly a passenger ticket: whoever's name is on the first line is bound to the booth and to a car that comes for them at the bell. Pruitt escaped his own ticket years ago by getting Teddy to sign, and then kept hiring, because the bridge is only ever freed of a keeper when a new one signs. Teddy, who tried to quit without a successor, was voided: stuck outside the booth, uncounted, knocking on the glass at 3:10 every night. Nell's double and her car were the bridge collecting her ticket. The only way to cancel it was to fill the seat with another name, which she did by sending Teddy across. That balanced the ledger and freed Teddy, but she signed the line, so she stays the keeper. She can only be released by getting someone else to sign, and by the end she is doing exactly what Pruitt did.

last_narration: Pruitt said Teddy quit weeks ago. And I had never told anyone my name tonight.
